questions.question: How is Hogwild! inference different from speculative decoding's within-sequence parallelism?
options: Several target models vote independently on a final answer.
Workers share one growing KV cache and see one another's tokens.
Several draft tokens are verified in one target pass within one sequence.
Several agents receive separate roles and report to a coordinator.
questions.explanation: Hogwild! parallelizes across several workers of the same model that append to one shared cache; each worker sees tokens from the others. Speculative decoding instead drafts multiple tokens within one sequence for a target model to verify.

questions.question: What shared resource lets Hogwild! workers notice work completed by other workers?
options: A replay buffer containing only completed final answers.
One shared cache reveals workers' newly written tokens.
A coordinator model that sends a summary after every round.
A separate private cache that hides each worker's generated tokens.
questions.explanation: The shared, growing KV cache is the coordination medium: a worker can read tokens another worker just wrote and choose a different sub-goal. Private caches or a coordinator-only summary would delay or hide that immediate shared context.

questions.question: In the lesson’s abstract timing example, T_serial=10,000 time steps, p=0.7, N=4, and c=200 time steps of coordination per worker. Using T*((1-p)+p/N)+c*N, what parallel time and speedup result?
options: 10000 steps and exactly 1.0x speedup.
5550 steps and about 1.8x speedup.
5350 steps, about 1.9x if only three workers are charged.
4750 steps and about 2.1x speedup.
questions.explanation: The stated model gives serial work 10000×(0.3+0.7/4)=4750 steps, then adds coordination 200×4=800, totaling 5550. Coordination is charged for all four workers, so speedup is 10000/5550≈1.80×; 4750 omits overhead and 5350 charges only three workers.

questions.question: Why does RoPE help workers read cache entries written at changing shared positions?
options: RoPE removes position information so tokens can be read in any order.
RoPE lets workers reuse cached entries at shared positions.
A token's learned absolute-position embedding is copied to every worker cache.
RoPE recomputes the full shared cache after every worker write.
questions.explanation: RoPE represents position through rotations in Q/K rather than a learned absolute-position vector. Under the lesson’s shared-cache setup, another worker can use the cached entry at its current shared position without rebuilding prior cache entries.

questions.question: A 1000-step chat task has p=0.3, N=4 workers, and c=200 overhead steps per worker. Using T*((1-p)+p/N)+c*N, what speedup should the team expect?
options: About 4.00x, because four workers share one cache.
About 1.29x, so parallel work outweighs all overhead.
About 2.50x, from dividing the serial time by four.
About 0.63x, so coordination makes it slower than serial.
questions.explanation: Parallel work takes 1000×(0.7+0.3/4)=775 steps, but coordination is charged for all four workers: 200×4=800, for 1575 total. Speedup is 1000/1575≈0.63×, below one; the short task cannot amortize that overhead.

questions.question: A reasoning task is mostly one linear proof, so workers repeatedly produce redundant tokens. Which deployment choice fits the lesson?
options: Use one worker when sub-goals are mostly sequential.
Use Hogwild! only after assigning every worker a different final answer.
Increase worker count, because shared-cache visibility removes all redundancy.
Increase coordination overhead so the workers explore longer.
questions.explanation: Hogwild! helps when a task has independent sub-goals workers can cover without repeating one another. A mostly sequential proof offers little parallel fraction, so extra workers add cache-reading and coordination overhead without producing independent progress.
